clue.text: Deduce conclusions of Abaddon, Gehenna, Hell — such places

definitions.text: Deduce conclusions of Abaddon, Gehenna, Hell — such places

parts.note: to deduce is to infer

indicators.note: the conclusions of the three named places are their final letters

explanation.surface: A theological catalogue of the underworld's various names.
explanation.walkthrough: 'conclusions of' takes the last letters of Abaddon, Gehenna and Hell: N, A, L. The whole clue also defines: the word describes such hellish places.
explanation.definitionFit: Abaddon, Gehenna and Hell are all names for the underworld, and the adjective describes anything belonging to such regions.

clue.text: Measures taken over last month's affronts

indicators.note: in a down clue the first piece is placed over the second

parts.note: INS is short for inches, measures of length
ult., ultimo, means of last month, here with its possessive S

explanation.surface: Ruler readings from the previous month cause offence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taken over' puts INS above ULTS in the down light. ULT (ultimo) is old business-letter usage for last month.
explanation.definitionFit: Insults are slights or offensive remarks, the same as affronts.

clue.text: What Smith advocated to enlarge business

parts.note: to enlarge a prisoner is an old sense of setting free
business is trade

explanation.surface: An economist calling for growth in commerce.
explanation.walkthrough: Smith is Adam Smith, the economist of The Wealth of Nations. 'enlarge' is used in its old sense of releasing from prison.
explanation.definitionFit: Adam Smith argued for commerce without tariffs or protection between nations.

clue.text: Took fresh aim, say, in new position

indicators.note: say signals that the word for taking fresh aim is spoken, not spelt

parts.note: to take fresh aim is to re-sight a gun

explanation.surface: A marksman adjusted his sights after moving.
explanation.definitionFit: Something moved to another place has been relocated.

clue.text: Bill, with the start of classes, I'm dying from lassitude

parts.note: AC (account) is a bill

indicators.note: the start of the word classes is its first letter

parts.note: I'm dying, said as I die

explanation.surface: Faced with a bill and lessons beginning, someone is perishing of weariness.
explanation.walkthrough: Accidie is the medieval sin of sloth, a spiritual torpor.
explanation.definitionFit: Accidie is apathy or listlessness, the same weary state as lassitude.

clue.text: Packing-case meant for Sydney

explanation.surface: A crate destined for an Australian city.
explanation.walkthrough: Sydney is not the city but Sydney Carton, the hero who goes to the guillotine in Dickens's A Tale of Two Cities.
explanation.definitionFit: A cardboard box used for packing; also the surname of Dickens's Sydney in A Tale of Two Cities.

clue.text: It's a plant! Nora cried out

indicators.note: out suggests the letters of the two words are put out of order

explanation.surface: Nora exclaims on spotting a herb.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' reads as Nora crying out, but it signals the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: Coriander is an aromatic herb, so a kind of plant.

clue.text: Tell composer Lawrence's other name in one

parts.note: T. E. Lawrence enlisted in the RAF under the name Ross
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Asking someone to reveal the alias Lawrence used.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tell' is not a verb but William Tell, the opera whose composer is meant.
explanation.definitionFit: Rossini wrote the opera William Tell, so he is its composer.

clue.text: Mrs Woolf's romance with Roland in Italy

explanation.surface: Virginia Woolf has an affair with Roland on an Italian trip.
explanation.walkthrough: Virginia Woolf's novel Orlando is a fantastical biography; Orlando is also the Italian form of Roland, hero of Orlando Furioso.
explanation.definitionFit: Title of Virginia Woolf's 1928 novel; also the Italian name of Charlemagne's paladin.

clue.text: Material showing the prophet a dupe

parts.note: a prophet is a seer
a dupe is a sucker, someone easily fooled

explanation.surface: Fabric that reveals the soothsayer as a fool.
explanation.definitionFit: Seersucker is a puckered cotton fabric, so it is a kind of material.

clue.text: The place for bargains is in Greater Manchester

explanation.surface: Telling shoppers where to find cheap goods in north-west England.
explanation.walkthrough: Sale is a town in Greater Manchester, a county in north-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: A clearance event is where goods are cut-price; also a town near Manchester.

clue.text: His world — wide liberal beliefs linking East and West?

definitions.text: His world — wide liberal beliefs linking East and West?

parts.words: His world — wide liberal beliefs linking East and West?
parts.note: a person of broad-minded religious views; the lines running east to west around the globe hint at the first part of the word

explanation.surface: A man whose tolerant philosophy bridges Oriental and Occidental thought.
explanation.walkthrough: Lines of latitude run east and west round the world, while the whole word means a broad-minded churchman.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone tolerant of a wide range of views, especially in religion, holds broad liberal beliefs.

clue.text: Dawdles, wandering about — so wrap up!

indicators.note: wandering about suggests the letters of the preceding word roam into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone dawdling around is told to wrap up warm.
explanation.definitionFit: To swathe a baby tightly in cloth is to wrap it up.

clue.text: Far from maturing and very old-fashioned

explanation.surface: Describing something both immature and hopelessly outdated.
explanation.walkthrough: A long-dated bond or bill does not mature for many years; split as two words it means badly out of date.
explanation.definitionFit: A security with a distant redemption date is not close to maturity; also, read as long out of fashion.

clue.text: Give new issue to old journalist

annotationWithheld.why: Give new issue to old journalist (7): ADDISON is ADD + SON, but no clue word gives the I; neither the scan nor a search shows a missing word.
annotationWithheld.clue: Give new issue to old journalist

clue.text: By inclination I want less variety

indicators.note: variety asks for a different arrangement of the three preceding words' letters

explanation.surface: Someone says that, by preference, they would like fewer kinds of thing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'By inclination' looks like 'by preference', but it means at a slant.
explanation.definitionFit: Something placed at an angle or slope is aslant, on an inclination.

clue.text: Were his novels profound in key?

definitions.text: Were his novels profound in key?

parts.note: profound means deep
G is a musical key

explanation.surface: A critic wonders whether a writer's books had depth.
explanation.walkthrough: Warwick Deeping was a popular English novelist of the 1920s, best known for Sorrell and Son.
explanation.definitionFit: The question points to a novelist whose surname suits a writer of profound books.

clue.text: Involve me in return with transport authority fuel

indicators.note: in return tells us the word me is read backwards

parts.note: taken as written
BR is British Rail, the former railway authority
oil is a fuel

explanation.surface: A complaint about the railway's fuel getting a passenger mixed up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in return' turns ME into EM. BR (British Rail) ran Britain's railways until privatisation in the 1990s.
explanation.definitionFit: To embroil someone is to drag them into a dispute, to involve them.

clue.text: Unique time for a gift

explanation.surface: Wondering about a special moment to hand over a gift.
explanation.walkthrough: The present moment is unique, the only time that exists now.
explanation.definitionFit: The current moment, distinct from past and future; also something given.

clue.text: Might it have been useful as floodlight, say?

definitions.text: Might it have been useful as floodlight, say?

parts.words: Might it have been useful as floodlight, say?
parts.note: a bright electric light; read as Noah's boat during the Flood, its light would have been a flood light

explanation.surface: Wondering whether a lamp would serve to light a stadium.
explanation.walkthrough: The first part sounds like Noah's ark, so a lamp on it would have lit the Flood.
explanation.definitionFit: This powerful electric light, using a spark between electrodes, was once used for floodlighting and searchlights.

clue.text: State alternatives both available to artillery

parts.note: and/or offers both alternatives together
RA is the Royal Artillery

explanation.surface: A country declares both options open to its gunners.
explanation.definitionFit: Andorra is a small independent country in the Pyrenees, a sovereign state.

clue.text: Bravery of Brecht's mother

explanation.surface: A tribute to the boldness of a playwright's parent.
explanation.walkthrough: Mother Courage is the heroine of Brecht's play Mother Courage and Her Children.
explanation.definitionFit: Valour or boldness; also the name of Brecht's canteen-woman heroine.

clue.text: Drinks for the bearers

explanation.surface: Refreshments laid on for those carrying the luggage.
explanation.definitionFit: Dark beers brewed from roasted malt; also people who carry loads.

clue.text: Like Mr Collins's letter, or livelihood

explanation.surface: Comparing a pompous letter of thanks with earning a living.
explanation.walkthrough: Mr Collins in Pride and Prejudice sends a thank-you note after staying at Longbourn, the kind called a bread-and-butter letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A thank-you letter for hospitality carries this name; the phrase also means one's basic income.

clue.text: Bishop of Oxford in Kensington?

explanation.surface: Asking whether a cleric from Oxford lives in a London district.
explanation.walkthrough: Charles Gore was Bishop of Oxford; Kensington Gore is a street in west London by the Royal Albert Hall.
explanation.definitionFit: Surname of the Edwardian Bishop Charles Gore; also the street name in Kensington, London.

clue.text: Gem of a trip to US state, lake included

parts.note: a trip is a tour

indicators.note: included tells us the lake goes within the state

parts.note: Maine is a US state
L is the map abbreviation for lake

explanation.surface: A precious stone bought on a holiday to America's lake country.
explanation.definitionFit: Tourmaline is a crystalline mineral cut as a gemstone.

clue.text: Groovy bellows — mender takes note

parts.note: Francis Flute is the bellows-mender in Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream
D is a musical note

explanation.surface: A trendy repairman of bellows gets a message.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Groovy' is not slang for cool here: fluted columns have grooves. Flute is one of the mechanicals in A Midsummer Night's Dream.
explanation.definitionFit: Fluting is a set of parallel channels cut in a surface, so a fluted column is grooved.

clue.text: How Worthing's loss of both parents looked to Lady Bracknell

definitions.text: How Worthing's loss of both parents looked to Lady Bracknell

parts.words: How Worthing's loss of both parents looked to Lady Bracknell
parts.note: in The Importance of Being Earnest Lady Bracknell says that losing both parents looks like negligence

explanation.surface: Literary quiz on a famous line from Wilde's comedy.
explanation.walkthrough: Lady Bracknell tells Jack Worthing that to lose one parent may be a misfortune, but to lose both looks like carelessness.
explanation.definitionFit: Losing things through negligence is lack of attention, which is what she saw in losing two parents.
